title: Indexes, Triggers, and Functions
description: Speed up queries with indexes, automate logic with triggers, and encapsulate computations with user-defined functions.

data.text: This lesson covers three powerful but advanced database objects: indexes (the engine of query speed), triggers (code that fires automatically), and functions (reusable logic you call like a built-in).

An index is a data structure that lets SQL Server find rows without scanning the entire table. Think of it like a book's index — instead of reading every page, you look up a term and jump to the right page.

data.caption: Clustered index determines the physical order of rows; nonclustered index stores a separate lookup structure
data.definition:
flowchart LR
  sub1[Heap Table\n(rows in no particular order)] --> CI[Clustered Index\n(physical sort by key)]--> Scan[Table Scan\nO(n) — slow]
  sub1 --> NC[Nonclustered Index\n(separate lookup)]--> Seek[Index Seek\nO(log n) — fast]
  CI --> Seek2[Index Seek on clustered key\nO(log n) — fast]

  style Scan fill:#ffebee
  style Seek fill:#e8f5e9
  style Seek2 fill:#e8f5e9

data.title: Creating indexes
data.code:
-- Clustered index (or rely on PRIMARY KEY for this)
CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_products_category
ON production.products (category_id);

-- Nonclustered index with included columns
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_orders_customer_date
ON sales.orders (customer_id)
INCLUDE (order_date, order_status);

data.title: Included columns
data.text: Nonclustered indexes can carry non-key columns with the INCLUDE clause. This covers more queries from the index alone — no trip back to the main table. But every included column adds size, so be selective.

A trigger is a stored procedure that fires automatically when a specific event occurs — typically INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE on a table. There are two kinds: DML triggers (fire on data changes) and DDL triggers (fire on structural changes like CREATE TABLE or DROP INDEX).

data.title: DML trigger preventing deletion of protected rows
data.code:
CREATE TRIGGER trg_PreventProductDelete
ON production.products
FOR DELETE
AS
BEGIN
    IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM deleted WHERE is_protected = 1)
    BEGIN
        RAISERROR('Cannot delete protected products.', 16, 1);
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    END
END;

data.title: Triggers can cause cascading effects
data.text: Because triggers fire automatically, a poorly written one can cause cascading updates, infinite loops, or unexpected slowdowns. Keep triggers simple and test them thoroughly with real workloads.

A user-defined function (UDF) is a reusable routine that returns a value or a table. Scalar functions return a single value; table-valued functions return a result set. Unlike stored procedures, functions can be called inside SELECT, WHERE, and other expressions.

data.title: Scalar function
Inline table-valued function
data.code:
CREATE FUNCTION Sales.GetCustomerOrders(@CustomerID INT)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN
    SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status
    FROM   sales.orders
    WHERE  customer_id = @CustomerID;

data.title: Functions must be deterministic
data.text: Functions cannot perform data modifications (no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) and should not call non-deterministic functions. This is enforced by SQL Server — if a function tries to modify data, it raises an error.

data.title: Database objects essentials
points: Clustered index = one per table, defines physical row order; nonclustered = separate lookup structure
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX with INCLUDE to cover more queries from the index
Triggers fire automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (DML) or schema changes (DDL)
Functions return a value or table and can be used in expressions — but must not modify data
